claim: Emotional arousal, a process mediated by the amygdala, can enhance attention to stimuli in a non-spatial manner.
source: Emotional arousal, a process mediated by the amygdala, can enhance attention to stimuli in a non-spatial manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the amygdala's role in emotional arousal and attention.

claim: Amygdala neural activity was recently shown to encode spatial information about reward-predictive stimuli.
source: However, amygdala neural activity was recently shown to encode spatial information about reward-predictive stimuli, and to correlate with spatial attention allocation.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Amygdala neural activity correlates with spatial attention allocation.
source: However, amygdala neural activity was recently shown to encode spatial information about reward-predictive stimuli, and to correlate with spatial attention allocation.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings about the relationship between amygdala activity and spatial attention.

claim: Neural responses in the amygdala encoded spatial information similarly for stimuli associated with both reward and punishment.
source: Neural responses encoded spatial information similarly for stimuli associated with both valences of reinforcement, and responses reflected spatial attention allocation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Amygdala neural responses reflected spatial attention allocation to both reward-predicting and punishment-threatening stimuli.
source: Neural responses encoded spatial information similarly for stimuli associated with both valences of reinforcement, and responses reflected spatial attention allocation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the study.

claim: The amygdala may act to enhance spatial attention to sensory stimuli associated with rewarding or aversive experiences.
source: The amygdala therefore may act to enhance spatial attention to sensory stimuli associated with rewarding or aversive experiences.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Inherently emotional stimuli can enhance spatial attention.
source: Inherently emotional stimuli and stimuli that have acquired emotional meaning through learning can enhance spatial attention (Armony and Dolan, 2002; Maunsell, 2004; Anderson, 2005; Phelps et al., 2006; Peck et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Stimuli that have acquired emotional meaning through learning can enhance spatial attention.
source: Inherently emotional stimuli and stimuli that have acquired emotional meaning through learning can enhance spatial attention (Armony and Dolan, 2002; Maunsell, 2004; Anderson, 2005; Phelps et al., 2006; Peck et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Enhanced spatial attention improves sensory processing of behaviorally relevant stimuli.
source: Enhanced spatial attention improves sensory processing of behaviorally relevant stimuli (Anderson et al., 2011) and quickens purposeful actions based on these stimuli (Posner, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2011.

claim: Enhanced spatial attention quickens purposeful actions based on behaviorally relevant stimuli.
source: Enhanced spatial attention improves sensory processing of behaviorally relevant stimuli (Anderson et al., 2011) and quickens purposeful actions based on these stimuli (Posner, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Posner, 1980.

claim: The amygdala is a brain area traditionally linked to emotional processes.
source: The amygdala, a brain area traditionally linked to emotional processes (LeDoux, 2000; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Murray, 2007; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010), may play an important role in enhancing spatial attention to emotional stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The amygdala may play an important role in enhancing spatial attention to emotional stimuli.
source: The amygdala, a brain area traditionally linked to emotional processes (LeDoux, 2000; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Murray, 2007; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010), may play an important role in enhancing spatial attention to emotional stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research and the current study's findings.

claim: The amygdala is important in processing aversive stimuli.
source: A substantial body of literature has documented the amygdala's importance in processing both aversive (Campeau and Davis, 1995; Quirk et al., 1995) and appetitive stimuli (Sanghera et al., 1979; Nishijo et al., 1988; Holland and Gallagher, 1993; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Baxter and Murray, 2002; Carelli et al., 2003; Sugase-Miyamoto and Richmond, 2005; Ambroggi et al., 2008; Tye et al., 2008; Shabel and Janak, 2009; Bermudez and Schultz, 2010; Jenison et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The amygdala is important in processing appetitive stimuli.
source: A substantial body of literature has documented the amygdala's importance in processing both aversive (Campeau and Davis, 1995; Quirk et al., 1995) and appetitive stimuli (Sanghera et al., 1979; Nishijo et al., 1988; Holland and Gallagher, 1993; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Baxter and Murray, 2002; Carelli et al., 2003; Sugase-Miyamoto and Richmond, 2005; Ambroggi et al., 2008; Tye et al., 2008; Shabel and Janak, 2009; Bermudez and Schultz, 2010; Jenison et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Amygdala neurons often responded differentially to conditioned stimuli depending on whether they predicted a positive or negative outcome.
source: Recent studies have compared amygdala neural responses to the same conditioned stimulus (CS) when paired with a rewarding or aversive unconditioned stimulus (US); neurons often responded differentially to the CS depending on whether it predicted a positive or negative outcome (Paton et al., 2006; Belova et al., 2007, 2008; Morrison et al., 2011) suggestive of a valence-specific coding scheme where neurons respond to stimuli on a 'good-to-bad' scale.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Different populations of amygdala neurons fired more for either reward- or punishment-predicting stimuli.
source: Further, different populations of neurons fired more for either reward- or punishment-predicting stimuli, raising the possibility that the amygdala contains distinct networks for processing stimuli possessing appetitive and aversive associations (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The amygdala may contain distinct networks for processing stimuli possessing appetitive and aversive associations.
source: Further, different populations of neurons fired more for either reward- or punishment-predicting stimuli, raising the possibility that the amygdala contains distinct networks for processing stimuli possessing appetitive and aversive associations (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research findings.

claim: Distinct appetitive and aversive circuits in the amygdala are causally related to valence-specific behavior.
source: Indeed, a recent study has now documented that distinct appetitive and aversive circuits in the amygdala are causally related to valence-specific behavior (Redondo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Redondo et al., 2014.

claim: The firing rates of amygdala neurons are correlated in some circumstances with valence-nonspecific aspects of conditioned stimuli.
source: Prior studies indicate that the firing rates of amygdala neurons are correlated in some circumstances with valence-nonspecific aspects of conditioned (Shabel and Janak, 2009) and unconditioned stimuli (Belova et al., 2007), suggesting that the amygdala could modulate arousal or related processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The firing rates of amygdala neurons are correlated in some circumstances with valence-nonspecific aspects of unconditioned stimuli.
source: Prior studies indicate that the firing rates of amygdala neurons are correlated in some circumstances with valence-nonspecific aspects of conditioned (Shabel and Janak, 2009) and unconditioned stimuli (Belova et al., 2007), suggesting that the amygdala could modulate arousal or related processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The amygdala could modulate arousal or related processes.
source: Prior studies indicate that the firing rates of amygdala neurons are correlated in some circumstances with valence-nonspecific aspects of conditioned (Shabel and Janak, 2009) and unconditioned stimuli (Belova et al., 2007), suggesting that the amygdala could modulate arousal or related processes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research findings.

claim: Nearly all previous studies have assumed that if the amygdala modulates valence-nonspecific processes, it does so in a non-spatial manner.
source: Nearly all previous studies have assumed that if the amygdala modulates valence-nonspecific processes, it does so in a non-spatial manner (Holland and Gallagher, 1999; Maddux et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Amygdala neurons encode information about both the spatial location and reward association of visual stimuli.
source: Amygdala neurons encode information about both the spatial location and reward association of visual stimuli (Peck et al., 2013; Peck and Salzman, 2014), and the maintenance of coordinated amygdala signals representing space and reward is task dependent (Peck et al., In press).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: The maintenance of coordinated amygdala signals representing space and reward is task dependent.
source: Amygdala neurons encode information about both the spatial location and reward association of visual stimuli (Peck et al., 2013; Peck and Salzman, 2014), and the maintenance of coordinated amygdala signals representing space and reward is task dependent (Peck et al., In press).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The encoding of space and reward in the primate amygdala has been confirmed by human neuroimaging data.
source: The encoding of space and reward in the primate amygdala has now also been confirmed by human neuroimaging data (Ousdal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ousdal et al., 2014.

claim: Amygdala neural activity is correlated with saccadic reaction times to a barely perceptible target.
source: Furthermore, amygdala neural activity is correlated with a behavioral measure of spatial attention, saccadic reaction times to a barely perceptible target (Peck et al., 2013; Peck and Salzman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: Correlations between reaction time and amygdala activity have a different sign depending upon the location of the target.
source: Correlations between reaction time and amygdala activity have a different sign depending upon the location of the target, with increased activity predicting shorter reaction times to some locations and longer reaction times to other locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research findings.

claim: An intact amygdala is vital for guiding gaze towards emotionally-relevant features of fearful face stimuli in humans.
source: In humans, an intact amygdala is vital for guiding gaze towards emotionally-relevant features of fearful face stimuli (Adolphs et al., 2005) and for augmenting BOLD responses to these stimuli in the ventral visual areas (Vuilleumier et al., 2004) that receive amygdalar input (Amaral and Price, 1984) and play an important role in attentional processing (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adolphs et al., 2005.

claim: An intact amygdala is vital for augmenting BOLD responses to fearful face stimuli in the ventral visual areas in humans.
source: In humans, an intact amygdala is vital for guiding gaze towards emotionally-relevant features of fearful face stimuli (Adolphs et al., 2005) and for augmenting BOLD responses to these stimuli in the ventral visual areas (Vuilleumier et al., 2004) that receive amygdalar input (Amaral and Price, 1984) and play an important role in attentional processing (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vuilleumier et al., 2004.

claim: Ventral visual areas receive amygdalar input.
source: In humans, an intact amygdala is vital for guiding gaze towards emotionally-relevant features of fearful face stimuli (Adolphs et al., 2005) and for augmenting BOLD responses to these stimuli in the ventral visual areas (Vuilleumier et al., 2004) that receive amygdalar input (Amaral and Price, 1984) and play an important role in attentional processing (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amaral and Price, 1984.

claim: Ventral visual areas play an important role in attentional processing.
source: In humans, an intact amygdala is vital for guiding gaze towards emotionally-relevant features of fearful face stimuli (Adolphs et al., 2005) and for augmenting BOLD responses to these stimuli in the ventral visual areas (Vuilleumier et al., 2004) that receive amygdalar input (Amaral and Price, 1984) and play an important role in attentional processing (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004.

claim: Unilateral amygdala lesions are associated with decreased selectivity for negatively valenced stimuli in ipsilateral visual cortices.
source: Moreover, neuroimaging data has revealed that unilateral amygdala lesions are associated with decreased selectivity for negatively valenced stimuli in ipsilateral visual cortices (Vuilleumier et al., 2004), a finding consistent with amygdalar projections to visual cortex being primarily ipsilateral (Iwai and Yukie, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vuilleumier et al., 2004.

claim: Amygdalar projections to visual cortex are primarily ipsilateral.
source: Moreover, neuroimaging data has revealed that unilateral amygdala lesions are associated with decreased selectivity for negatively valenced stimuli in ipsilateral visual cortices (Vuilleumier et al., 2004), a finding consistent with amygdalar projections to visual cortex being primarily ipsilateral (Iwai and Yukie, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iwai and Yukie, 1987.

claim: The pathway from the amygdala to ventral visual areas may be important in guiding spatial attention towards stimuli associated with both rewarding and aversive outcomes.
source: Thus, the pathway from the amygdala to ventral visual areas may be important in guiding spatial attention towards stimuli associated with both rewarding and aversive outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research findings.

claim: 186 single units and 159 multi-unit sites were recorded from the left amygdala of two monkeys.
source: During task performance, we recorded the extracellular action potentials of 186 single units (SUA) and 159 multi-unit sites (MUA) from the left amygdala of two monkeys (monkey L: 46 SUA, 45 MUA; monkey O: 140 SUA, 114 MUA).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collection.

claim: When the target appeared at the reward cue location relative to either the punishment cue or neutral cue location, hit rate was greater.
source: When the target appeared at the reward cue location relative to either the punishment cue or neutral cue location (R/P & R/N trials), or when the target appeared at the punishment cue location relative to the neutral cue location (P/N trials), hit rate was greater (Figure 2A; χ2-test, P << 10−4), reaction time was shorter (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon, p < 10−23), and false alarm frequency was greater (i.e. frequency of saccades to a cue location before the target appeared; Figure 2C; χ2-test, P << 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: When the target appeared at the punishment cue location relative to the neutral cue location, hit rate was greater.
source: When the target appeared at the reward cue location relative to either the punishment cue or neutral cue location (R/P & R/N trials), or when the target appeared at the punishment cue location relative to the neutral cue location (P/N trials), hit rate was greater (Figure 2A; χ2-test, P << 10−4), reaction time was shorter (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon, p < 10−23), and false alarm frequency was greater (i.e. frequency of saccades to a cue location before the target appeared; Figure 2C; χ2-test, P << 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: When the target appeared at the reward or punishment cue location (relative to neutral), reaction time was shorter.
source: When the target appeared at the reward cue location relative to either the punishment cue or neutral cue location (R/P & R/N trials), or when the target appeared at the punishment cue location relative to the neutral cue location (P/N trials), hit rate was greater (Figure 2A; χ2-test, P << 10−4), reaction time was shorter (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon, p < 10−23), and false alarm frequency was greater (i.e. frequency of saccades to a cue location before the target appeared; Figure 2C; χ2-test, P << 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: When the target appeared at the reward or punishment cue location (relative to neutral), false alarm frequency was greater.
source: When the target appeared at the reward cue location relative to either the punishment cue or neutral cue location (R/P & R/N trials), or when the target appeared at the punishment cue location relative to the neutral cue location (P/N trials), hit rate was greater (Figure 2A; χ2-test, P << 10−4), reaction time was shorter (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon, p < 10−23), and false alarm frequency was greater (i.e. frequency of saccades to a cue location before the target appeared; Figure 2C; χ2-test, P << 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The location of the reward cue had a strong influence on firing rates such that many sites responded differentially on R-contra and R-ipsi trials.
source: The location of the reward cue had a strong influence on firing rates such that many sites in each time window responded differentially on R-contra and R-ipsi trials (Table 1; Figure 3B); this population included sites that had significantly greater (spatial-reward selectivity index >0.5) or lesser (index <0.5) firing rates when the reward cue appeared contralaterally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3B.

claim: The overall reward predicted by the cues influenced firing rates.
source: The overall reward predicted by the cues influenced firing rates as well (Table 1; Figure 3B); firing rates were often significantly higher (reward selectivity index >0.5) or lower (index <0.5) when the reward cue was presented (R-present trials) than when it was absent (R-absent trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3B.

claim: Sites often fired differentially between P-contra and P-ipsi trials.
source: Sites often fired differentially between P-contra and P-ipsi trial (Table 1; Figure 3B), with sites firing significantly more (spatial-punishment selectivity index >0.5) or less (index <0.5) on P-contra trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3B.

claim: Spatial-punishment selectivity was generally weaker than spatial-reward selectivity.
source: In agreement with the relatively small effect the punishment cue had on behavior as compared to the reward cue (Figure 2), spatial-punishment selectivity was generally weaker than spatial-reward selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with behavioral results in Figure 2.

claim: The population of spatial-punishment selective sites was significantly smaller than the population of spatial-reward selective sites.
source: The population of spatial-punishment selective sites was significantly smaller than the population of spatial-reward selective sites (χ2-test, p < 10−4 for each time window), and the magnitude of spatial-reward selectivity was significantly greater than that of spatial-punishment selectivity (compare |ROC—0.5|; Paired Wilcoxon, p < 10−5 in each time epoch).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of spatial-reward selectivity was significantly greater than that of spatial-punishment selectivity.
source: The population of spatial-punishment selective sites was significantly smaller than the population of spatial-reward selective sites (χ2-test, p < 10−4 for each time window), and the magnitude of spatial-reward selectivity was significantly greater than that of spatial-punishment selectivity (compare |ROC—0.5|; Paired Wilcoxon, p < 10−5 in each time epoch).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a strong, positive relationship between reward selectivity and spatial-reward selectivity that was significant in each time epoch.
source: Consistent with our previous results (Peck et al., 2013), we found a strong, positive relationship between reward selectivity and spatial-reward selectivity that was significant in each time epoch (Figure 4A; linear regression, p < 10−32), indicating that those sites that fired more when the reward cue was present tended to fire more when that reward cue appeared contralaterally.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Sites that fired more when the reward cue was present tended to fire more when that reward cue appeared contralaterally.
source: Consistent with our previous results (Peck et al., 2013), we found a strong, positive relationship between reward selectivity and spatial-reward selectivity that was significant in each time epoch (Figure 4A; linear regression, p < 10−32), indicating that those sites that fired more when the reward cue was present tended to fire more when that reward cue appeared contralaterally.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: There was a clear positive relationship between spatial selectivity for reward and punishment cues in each time epoch.
source: We observed a clear positive relationship between spatial selectivity for reward and punishment cues in each time epoch (Figure 4B; linear regression, p = 1.6*10−22, 0.0001, 0.0007 in the 100–400 ms, 400–700 ms, and 700–1000 ms epochs, respectively); these regression slopes were statistically indistinguishable between monkeys (ANCOVA, p = 0.10, 0.59, 0.74 for each time window) and between SUA/MUA (p = 0.51, 0.59, 0.65).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Of those responses with significant spatial-reward and spatial punishment selectivity, the sign of selectivity was the same for 84%.
source: Of those responses (i.e. for each site and time window) with significant spatial-reward and spatial punishment selectivity (n = 64), the sign of selectivity was the same for 54 (84%; Binomial-test, p < 10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Hit rate was higher when the target appeared at the P cue location on R/P trials than when it appeared at the N cue location on R/N trials.
source: We compared R/P and R/N trials and found that hit rate was higher when the target appeared at the P cue location on R/P trials than when it appeared at the N cue location on R/N trials (Figure 5A; χ2-test, p < 10−4); this effect was similar for both monkeys (monkey O: p < 10−4; monkey L: p = 0.0696).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Spatial-reward and punishment-contra selectivity indices were positively correlated.
source: Across recordings, spatial-reward and punishment-contra selectivity indices were positively correlated (Figure 5D; linear regression, p = 0.0012, 0.0082, 0.0439 in each time epoch) indicating that those sites firing more when an R cue appeared contralaterally tended to fire more when a contralateral P cue (as opposed to a contralateral N cue) appeared with an ipsilateral R cue; time epoch did not have a significant effect on the slope of these regressions (ANCOVA, p = 0.83).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Spatial-reward and punishment-ipsi selectivity indices were negatively correlated in the 700–1000 ms epoch.
source: Strikingly, spatial-reward and punishment-ipsi selectivity indices were negatively correlated (as opposed to the positive correlation observed between spatial-reward and punishment-contra indices) in the 700–100 ms epoch (Figure 5E; p = 0.0009; p = 0.59, 0.59 in the 100–400 and 400–700 ms epochs, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 5E.

claim: The inclusion of the R cue tended to decrease the frequency of aborts.
source: For each monkey, the inclusion of the R cue tended to decrease the frequency of aborts (Figure 6, compare R/P vs P/N trials; Bonferroni-corrected χ2-test, p < 10−4 each for monkey).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 6.

claim: The inclusion of the P cue tended to increase the frequency of aborts.
source: In contrast, the inclusion of the P cue tended to increase the frequency of aborts (compare R/P vs R/N trials; p < 0.05 for each monkey).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Significant selectivity for aborts was more frequent than expected by chance on P-contra trials.
source: Significant selectivity for aborts was more frequent than expected by chance on P-contra trials (7.9%, 7.6%, 10.3% of neurons in each time epoch; Binomial-test, p < 0.0414, 0.0707, 0.0050; Figure 7A,B); the proportion of significantly selective neurons was greater than chance in the 100–400 ms epoch for R-contra trials as well (8.2%, p = 0.0469).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 7A,B.

claim: There was a statistically significant negative correlation between reward selectivity indices and abort selectivity indices on P-contra trials in all 3 time epochs.
source: We found a statistically significant negative correlation between reward selectivity indices and abort selectivity indices on P-contra trials in all 3 time epochs (Figure 7C, linear regression, p < 0.0006, 0.0066, 0.0030 for each time epoch); these relationships were statistically indistinguishable across monkeys (ANCOVA, p > 0.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 7C.

claim: Neurons that fire more strongly in a more rewarding situation tend to fire less on trials when a monkey breaks fixation.
source: Neurons that fire more strongly in a more rewarding situation (e.g. R/N trials) tend to fire less on trials when a monkey breaks fixation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on abort selectivity.

claim: Neurons that fire more strongly when a monkey is in a less rewarding situation fire more on trials when a monkey aborts.
source: By contrast, neurons that fire more strongly when a monkey is in a less rewarding situation (e.g. P/N trials), fire more on trials when a monkey aborts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on abort selectivity.

claim: Amygdala neurons not only register the emotional significance of stimuli promising reward and threatening aversive events, but they also represent information about the spatial location of those stimuli.
source: Amygdala neurons not only register the emotional significance of stimuli promising reward and threatening aversive events, but they also represent information about the spatial location of those stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The spatial representation in the amygdala may serve to link our emotional world to cognitive actions that promote our survival.
source: Given that the motivational significance and location of stimuli together bias spatial attention, the spatial representation in the amygdala may serve to link our emotional world to cognitive actions—the enhancement of spatial attention to relevant stimuli—that promote our survival.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: All materials and methods complied with the National Institutes of Health guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University.
source: All Materials and methods complied with the National Institutes of Health guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Two male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, 8–10 kg) were used in these experiments.
source: Two male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, 8–10 kg) were used in these experiments.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental subjects.

claim: Recordings from single neurons and multi-unit sites in the amygdala were made through a surgically implanted plastic cylinder affixed to the skull.
source: Recordings from single neurons (SUA) and multi-unit sites (MUA) in the amygdala were made through a surgically implanted plastic cylinder affixed to the skull.
evidence: This is a description of experimental methods.

claim: Four to eight electrodes were individually lowered into the left amygdala using a multiple electrode microdrive.
source: Four to eight electrodes were individually lowered into the left (monkeys O and L) amygdala using a multiple electrode microdrive (NaN Instruments, Nazareth, Israel).
evidence: This is a description of experimental methods.

claim: Monkeys were required to make a saccadic eye movement to the location of the target within 600 ms to complete the trial correctly.
source: The monkeys completed the trial correctly (a 'hit') by making a saccadic eye movement to the location of the target within 600 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task.

claim: 61% of miss trials occurred when the monkey failed to make a saccade at all.
source: Generally, 'miss' trials occurred when the monkey failed to make a saccade at all (61% of miss trials) since the timing of target onset was variable and the target itself was difficult to detect; however, miss trials also included those where a saccade was directed towards the location opposite the target (28% of incorrect trials) or elsewhere (11% of incorrect trials).
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data.

claim: 28% of miss trials occurred when a saccade was directed towards the location opposite the target.
source: Generally, 'miss' trials occurred when the monkey failed to make a saccade at all (61% of miss trials) since the timing of target onset was variable and the target itself was difficult to detect; however, miss trials also included those where a saccade was directed towards the location opposite the target (28% of incorrect trials) or elsewhere (11% of incorrect trials).
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data.

claim: 11% of miss trials occurred when a saccade was directed elsewhere.
source: Generally, 'miss' trials occurred when the monkey failed to make a saccade at all (61% of miss trials) since the timing of target onset was variable and the target itself was difficult to detect; however, miss trials also included those where a saccade was directed towards the location opposite the target (28% of incorrect trials) or elsewhere (11% of incorrect trials).
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data.

claim: Monkeys never received both a reward and a punishment on the same trial.
source: These contingencies meant that monkeys never received both a reward and a punishment on the same trial.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The contrast and size of the Gabor patch targets were adjusted online to maintain an overall performance level of approximately 70% correct.
source: Targets were Gabor patches; we adjusted the contrast and size of the Gabors online to maintain an overall performance level of ∼70% correct.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Theoretical chance performance was about 23%.
source: Because the interval during which the target could appear was long and the reaction time window was relatively short, theoretical chance performance was about 23%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental design.

claim: Behavioral and neural data was similar across cue sets.
source: Behavioral and neural data was similar across cue sets, so the data were combined except where noted.
evidence: This is a report of data analysis methods.

claim: The results were similar for MUA and SUA.
source: We combined MUA and SUA for all our analyses since the results were similar for each; we address this similarity below with respect to the specific analyses.
evidence: This is a report of data analysis methods and findings.

claim: The vast majority of recordings were in the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala.
source: As with previous work (Peck et al., 2013), we estimated that the vast majority of our recordings were in the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala (n = 283) as opposed to the central nucleus (n = 51) or anterior amygdaloid area (n = 11).
evidence: This is a report of anatomical localization of recordings.
